files.samples/iyi/kemal/dsl.iyi: # Kemal's DSL, ported from `kemal/src/kemal/dsl.cr`. # # The original's first line is the whole problem: "Kemal DSL is defined here # and it's baked into global scope." `require "kemal"` injects `get`, `post` # and `before_all` into the importing program's namespace — the same action at # a distance as an open class, and also Kemal's entire identity. Making users # write `kemal.get "/" do ... end` would be safe and would kill the framework. # # `using` moves the decision to the consumer: the library exports names, and # the program says which ones it wants unqualified. See `webapp.iyi`. module kemal/dsl import kemal/router using kemal/router::{Router, Context, IntoBody} HTTP_METHODS = %w(get post put patch delete options head) # One application value, in place of `Kemal::RouteHandler::INSTANCE` and the # three singletons beside it. `router.cr:270` works around those being global # and mutable — "may have been cleared between tests" — and nothing about # separate compilation forced that; a clean sheet is just the moment to fix it. APP = Router.new {% for method in HTTP_METHODS %} pub def {{ method.id }}(path : String, &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody APP.{{ method.id }}(path, &block) end {% end %} pub def before_all(path : String = "*", &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody APP.before(path, &block) end pub def after_all(path : String = "*", &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody APP.after(path, &block) end pub def mount(path : String, router : Router) : Nil APP.mount(path, router) end pub def app : Router APP end
files.samples/iyi/kemal/router.iyi: # Kemal's modular router, ported to iyi from `kemal/src/kemal/router.cr` (337 # lines). This is the acceptance test the design named: the hardest DSL in the # Crystal ecosystem for "no open classes, no global macros". # # What is deliberately not ported, and why: # # * `HTTP::Server::Context`, WebSocket and SSE — they need the stdlib, and # they add no construct the routes do not already exercise. `Context` here # is a stub. # * `Kemal::RouteHandler::INSTANCE` and the other global mutable singletons. # `router.cr:270` carries a workaround for them — "may have been cleared # between tests" — and a clean sheet is the moment to stop. Registration # returns a value instead. module kemal/router pub struct Context getter method : String getter path : String def initialize(@method : String, @path : String) end end # The finding the port produced. Kemal types a route block as # `HTTP::Server::Context -> _` and coerces the result on every request: # # result = block.call(ctx) # result.is_a?(String) ? result : "" # router.cr:301 # # Mandatory export signatures forbid `_`, so the block's return type has to be # named — and once it is named, the coercion becomes a bound. The check moves # from every request to compile time, and a user can now make their own type # returnable by implementing the trait, which Kemal cannot offer. pub trait IntoBody abstract def into_body : String end impl IntoBody for String def into_body : String self end end impl IntoBody for Nil def into_body : String "" end end impl IntoBody for Int32 def into_body : String to_s end end HTTP_METHODS = %w(get post put patch delete options head) FILTER_METHODS = %w(get post put patch delete options) pub class Router alias Handler = Context -> String private record RouteDefinition, method : String, path : String, handler : Handler private record FilterDefinition, kind : Symbol, method : String, path : String, handler : Handler private record SubRouter, path : String, router : Router getter prefix : String @routes : Array(RouteDefinition) @filters : Array(FilterDefinition) @sub_routers : Array(SubRouter) def initialize(@prefix : String = "") @routes = [] of RouteDefinition @filters = [] of FilterDefinition @sub_routers = [] of SubRouter end # The macro loop ports unchanged — it reads a module-local constant and # emits declarations into its own module, which is legal under R-5. The one # addition is `forall B : IntoBody` on each generated signature. {% for method in HTTP_METHODS %} pub def {{ method.id }}(path : String, &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody add_route({{ method.upcase }}, path, &block) end {% end %} pub def before(path : String = "*", &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody add_filter(:before, "ALL", path, &block) end pub def after(path : String = "*", &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody add_filter(:after, "ALL", path, &block) end {% for method in FILTER_METHODS %} pub def before_{{ method.id }}(path : String = "*", &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody add_filter(:before, {{ method.upcase }}, path, &block) end pub def after_{{ method.id }}(path : String = "*", &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody add_filter(:after, {{ method.upcase }}, path, &block) end {% end %} # The sub-router arrives as a block parameter, and Kemal's original hands it # to the block as `self` instead — `with sub_router yield`. That is the one # thing about this port that reads worse than what it ports, so the reason is # here rather than in a commit message. # # R-2 asks an exported `def` to say what its block is (SPEC.md IV.2): the # body stays in this module, so a consumer reading only the signature has no # `yield` left to infer from. `& : Router -> Nil` says it. `with sub_router # yield` cannot be said at all — what makes it a DSL is that the block's # `self` changes, and `& : … -> …` has nowhere to write that down. # # So this is the rule costing something visible, and it is being paid rather # than avoided: a `namespace` that keeps `with` would have to stay unexported, # which is a worse trade for a DSL than one extra `|r|`. Giving `with … yield` # a notation is open (SPEC.md IV.2); until it has one, this is what an # exported block-taking method looks like. pub def namespace(path : String, & : Router -> Nil) : Nil sub_router = Router.new yield sub_router @sub_routers << SubRouter.new(path: path, router: sub_router) end pub def mount(path : String, router : Router) : Nil @sub_routers << SubRouter.new(path: path, router: router) end # Kemal's `register_routes` pushed into global singletons. This returns the # flattened table instead, which is the same walk without the globals. pub def routes(base_prefix : String = "") : Array(Tuple(String, String)) full_prefix = join_paths(base_prefix, @prefix) collected = [] of Tuple(String, String) @routes.each do |route| collected << {route.method, join_paths(full_prefix, route.path)} end @sub_routers.each do |sub| collected.concat(sub.router.routes(join_paths(full_prefix, sub.path))) end collected end # Ported from `register_filters`, which is the densest code in the file: # `case` on a symbol, `select` destructuring a tuple, `in?` over a splat, # and `starts_with?`. pub def filters_for(method : String, path : String) : Array(Symbol) applicable = [] of Symbol @filters.each do |filter| next unless filter.method.in?("ALL", method) matches = if filter.path == "*" true else scoped = join_paths(@prefix, filter.path) path == scoped || path.starts_with?("#{scoped}/") end next unless matches case filter.kind when :before then applicable << :before when :after then applicable << :after end end applicable end pub def dispatch(ctx : Context) : String before = 0 after = 0 filters_for(ctx.method, ctx.path).each do |kind| case kind when :before then before += 1 when :after then after += 1 end end body = "" @routes.each do |route| if route.method == ctx.method && join_paths(@prefix, route.path) == ctx.path body = route.handler.call(ctx) end end @sub_routers.each do |sub| body = sub.router.dispatch(ctx) if body.empty? end "#{before}|#{body}|#{after}" end private def add_route(method : String, path : String, &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody handler = ->(ctx : Context) { block.call(ctx).into_body } @routes << RouteDefinition.new(method: method, path: path, handler: handler) end private def add_filter(kind : Symbol, method : String, path : String, &block : Context -> B) : Nil forall B : IntoBody handler = ->(ctx : Context) { block.call(ctx).into_body } @filters << FilterDefinition.new(kind: kind, method: method, path: path, handler: handler) end private def join_paths(a : String, b : String) : String a = a.chomp('/') b = b.lchop('/') if b.starts_with?('/') return "/#{b}" if a.empty? return a if b.empty? "#{a}/#{b}" end end
files.samples/iyi/modules.iyi: # Modules across files: `import` and `using`. # # ./bin/crystal run samples/iyi/modules.iyi # # Everything below compiles and runs today. `hello.iyi` covers traits and # `impl` in a single file; this one covers the part a single file cannot show. module samples/modules # R-1: `import` names a module and loads it at most once, so the import graph # is a DAG rather than textual inclusion. It brings the module into scope # under its qualified name and nothing more — after this line, and with no # `using`, the module's names are reachable only as `App::Greeter::Greet` and # `App::Greeter.polite`. import app/greeter import app/formal # II.3: `using` is what makes those names available unqualified. It is written # by the consumer, not performed by the library: importing a module never # changes what the importer's unqualified names mean, so a library cannot # capture a name in your file by adding one to itself. using app/greeter # The selective form narrows a `using` to the names listed. Here it is not # decoration — `app/greeter` and `app/formal` both export `title`, and taking # both whole would make every unqualified `title` in this module ambiguous. using app/formal::{address} pub struct User getter name : String def initialize(@name : String) end end # `Greet` resolves through the `using` above, so `impl` needs no qualification. # # R-3's orphan rule allows this impl here because `User` is declared here: # this is the type's module. It would equally be allowed in `app/greeter`, # the trait's module. Nowhere else — a third module that imports both is # refused, which is what makes two modules unable to define the same impl. impl Greet for User def greet : String # `polite` comes from `app/greeter`, `address` from `app/formal`, and # `shout` is this module's own function, declared below. All three are # written the same way, because to this file they are all just names. shout(polite(name)) + " " + address(name) end end # A module's own functions are in scope for the types declared in it, without # `self.` and without qualification: an iyi module is a compilation unit, and # these are its functions. Not exported, so nothing outside can call it. def shout(text : String) : String text.upcase end puts User.new("iyi").greet # `title` was reachable unqualified from neither `using`: `app/greeter`'s was # left ambiguous by nothing (only one `using` was whole), and `app/formal`'s # was excluded by the selective form. Qualification always works. puts App::Greeter.title puts App::Formal.title # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # What this sample would report as an error # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # * Widening the second directive to `using app/formal` and then writing an # unqualified `title` is an error, and it is reported at the `title`, not at # the `using`. Widening it alone is not an error at all: two modules # exporting the same name is not by itself a mistake, so nothing is wrong # until a name is written that could mean either (SPEC.md II.3). # # * Adding `def title` here makes even that legal again. A local definition # beats a used one, silently, which is what keeps a library from breaking # its consumers by adding an export. # # * Moving the `impl` above into a module that is neither `app/greeter` nor # this one is refused by R-3, naming both modules where it would be allowed. # # * `using app/greeter::{greeting}` — `greeting` is declared there without # `pub`, so it is not part of the module's surface. The error names it at the # `using`, where the author can see which of the names they asked for they # cannot have. Widening to a bare `using app/greeter` does not reach it # either; it simply is not there to be found (R-2b). # # * `App::Greeter.greeting` — qualifying it does not get around `pub` either. # It has to be unreachable, not merely absent from `using`: `.iyimod` carries # a module's exports and nothing else, so if another module could call an # unmarked name, that metadata would not be enough to compile against # (SPEC.md IV.2). # # * `import app/v_1`, or any path segment that is not `[a-z][a-z0-9]*` with # single `_` between groups. A module declared `app/greeter` is reached as # `App::Greeter`, and the two notations are kept in step by making the # mapping reversible: the name splits back into a path at every upper-case # letter. `camelcase` drops an underscore before a digit, so `v_1` and `v1` # would both be `V1` — two paths naming one module (SPEC.md IV.6 #6). # # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Compiling this file without `app/greeter.iyi` # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # # R-1 says a module that imports another reads its `.iyimod` and never opens # its source. That is not a claim about a future release: # # ./bin/crystal build --no-codegen --emit-iyimod /tmp/mods samples/iyi/modules.iyi # ./bin/crystal mod dump --declarations /tmp/mods/app/greeter.iyimod # mv samples/iyi/app /tmp/app-elsewhere # ./bin/crystal build --use-iyimod /tmp/mods samples/iyi/modules.iyi # compiles # mv /tmp/app-elsewhere samples/iyi/app # # The second command prints what the third one compiles against: `app/greeter` # with `pub def polite(name : String) : String`, `pub trait Greet` with its # requirement, and no bodies at all. `greeting` is not in it — it carries no # `pub`, and R-2b's "unreachable rather than absent from `using`" is the same # statement as "not in the artifact". # # * Not yet: object code. `--use-iyimod` implies `--no-codegen`, because the # artifact carries what another module may call and not how it is done, so # there is nothing in it to generate a program from (SPEC.md IV.1f).
files.samples/iyi/sessions.iyi: # The first program that forgets - a table of who is signed in, which has # to lose an entry when somebody signs out. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/sessions.iyi # # A `Hash` kept insertion order from the day it arrived and could not # delete, because no program in this repository needed to; the header of # `src/iyi/hash.iyi` said so in as many words. This program needs to. # `delete` answers the value that was there, or `nil`, and the entries # that remain keep their order - so a person who signs out and back in # goes to the end of the table, which is what a table of arrivals means. # Like `basics`, `inventory`, `config`, `grid` and `shapes`, this documents # no rule: it is here because the prelude grows only when a program asks # (SPEC.md 0.1.0 item 3), and forgetting is what the sixth program does. module samples/sessions struct Session property user : String property since : Int32 # the tick the session opened on def initialize(@user : String, @since : Int32) end end class Table @open : Hash(String, Session) @tick : Int32 def initialize @open = {} of String => Session @tick = 0 end def sign_in(user : String) : Nil @tick = @tick + 1 @open[user] = Session.new(user, @tick) end # The session that closed, or nil when nobody by that name was in. def sign_out(user : String) : Session? @open.delete(user) end def show : Nil @open.each { |user, session| puts " #{user} since tick #{session.since}" } puts " (#{@open.size} signed in)" end end table = Table.new table.sign_in("ada") table.sign_in("linus") table.sign_in("grace") puts "three arrivals:" table.show # => ada, linus, grace; 3 signed in if gone = table.sign_out("linus") puts "linus left, had been in since tick #{gone.since}" # => tick 2 end table.show # => ada, grace; 2 signed in puts "nobody named bob: #{table.sign_out("bob").nil?}" # => true # Back in, and at the end: an entry that was deleted is a new arrival. table.sign_in("linus") puts "linus is back:" table.show # => ada, grace, linus; 3 signed in # Deleting everything and refilling, so the table's growth and its index # are exercised past the first page of entries. 20.times { |i| table.sign_in("guest#{i}") } 20.times { |i| table.sign_out("guest#{i}") } table.show # => ada, grace, linus; 3 signed in
files.samples/iyi/shapes.iyi: # The first program with a trait of its own - shapes that answer their # area, held in one list, added up - and the arithmetic around it. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/shapes.iyi # # `hello` documents what a trait is. This is the program a person writes # once they know: two structs behind one trait, a list typed by the trait, # and the small arithmetic a program like it reaches for - a rounded float, # a sum over a block, a number parsed that may fail, a power, a shift, a loop # that ends on a `break`. Like `basics`, `inventory`, `config` and `grid`, # it documents no rule; the prelude grows only when a program in this # repository needs something (SPEC.md 0.1.0 item 3). module samples/shapes trait Shape # A requirement says so: `abstract`. A plain `def` here opens a body. abstract def area : Float64 abstract def name : String end struct Circle def initialize(@radius : Float64) end end impl Shape for Circle def area : Float64 3.14159 * @radius * @radius end def name : String "circle" end end struct Rect def initialize(@width : Float64, @height : Float64) end end impl Shape for Rect def area : Float64 @width * @height end def name : String "rect" end end # 1. One list, two kinds, each asked the same question. shapes = [Circle.new(1.0), Rect.new(2.0, 3.0)] of Shape shapes.each { |shape| puts "#{shape.name}: #{shape.area.round(2)}" } # => circle: 3.14 # => rect: 6.0 puts shapes.sum { |shape| shape.area }.round(1) # => 9.1 puts shapes.max_by { |shape| shape.area }.name # => rect # 2. Numbers that arrive as text, some of them wrong. inputs = ["12", "x", "7", "-3"] parsed = inputs.map { |text| text.to_i? } puts parsed # => [12, nil, 7, -3] puts parsed.compact.sum # => 16 puts parsed.compact.map(&.abs) # => [12, 7, 3] # 3. Powers, shifts, and a loop that decides when to stop. puts 2 ** 10, 2.0 ** -2 # => 1024, 0.25 puts 1_i64 << 40 # => 1099511627776 puts 1024 >> 3 # => 128 side = 0 loop do side += 1 break if side * side > 50 end puts side # => 8
files.samples/iyi/socket.iyi: # Sockets: TCP client and server in one program on loopback. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/socket.iyi # # Binds to an ephemeral port (port 0), connects, exchanges a message each way, # prints what arrived, and closes cleanly. module samples/socket import std/socket using std/socket::{IyiSocket} # Server listens on an ephemeral port. The number the kernel picks is different # on every run, so it is used rather than printed: `bench/arena_exercise.sh` # runs every sample twice and asks for identical output, and a sample that # prints its port is a sample that can never answer that. server = IyiSocket.listen(0) port = server.local_port puts "server listening on an ephemeral port" # Client connects to server on loopback client = IyiSocket.connect("127.0.0.1", port) client.write("hello from client\n") # Server accepts and reads the message conn = server.accept msg = conn.read(1024) puts "server received: #{msg}" # Server replies to client conn.write("hello from server\n") reply = client.read(1024) puts "client received: #{reply}" # Clean teardown client.close conn.close server.close puts "closed"
files.samples/iyi/std_iterator.iyi: # The `std/iterator` port, demonstrated — lazy sequences. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/std_iterator.iyi # # `std/iterator.iyi` holds the `Iterator` trait and its lazy adaptors. # Unlike `Enumerable`, which processes sequences eagerly and creates intermediate # arrays at each step, `Iterator` transforms elements on demand when pulled. module samples/std_iterator import std/traits using std/traits::{Cmp, Num} import std/iterator using std/iterator::{Iterator, ArrayIterator} # An infinite sequence generator. Eagerly evaluating this would hang or OOM; # lazily evaluating it pulls only what the pipeline asks for. pub class NaturalNumbers getter pulls : Int32 def initialize @current = 1 @pulls = 0 end end impl Iterator for NaturalNumbers type Elem = Int32 def next : Int32? @pulls = @pulls + 1 val = @current @current = @current + 1 val end end # 1. Infinite sequence consumed finitely nats = NaturalNumbers.new first_five = nats.take(5).to_a puts "natural numbers first 5: #{first_five}" puts "pulls from generator: #{nats.pulls}" # 2. Composed lazy pipeline: square even naturals and take 4 # Eager evaluation would evaluate infinitely; lazy evaluation pulls only 8 items. nats2 = NaturalNumbers.new pipeline = nats2.select { |x| x % 2 == 0 } .map { |x| x * x } .take(4) .to_a puts "even squares first 4: #{pipeline}" puts "pulls for 4 matches: #{nats2.pulls}" # 3. Zipping and Chaining evens = Iterator.of([2, 4, 6]) odds = Iterator.of([1, 3, 5]) all_numbers = odds.chain(evens).to_a puts "chained odds and evens: #{all_numbers}" names = Iterator.of(["apple", "banana", "cherry"]) scores = Iterator.of([100, 95, 88]) pairs = names.zip(scores).to_a puts "zipped pairs: #{pairs}" # 4. Slicing and Windowing data = Iterator.of([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]) slices = data.each_slice(3).to_a puts "each_slice(3): #{slices}" window_source = Iterator.of([10, 20, 30, 40, 50]) windows = window_source.each_cons(3).to_a puts "each_cons(3): #{windows}" # 5. Stepping, Cycling, and Indexing stepped = Iterator.of([0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]).step(2).to_a puts "stepped by 2: #{stepped}" cycled = Iterator.of(["tick", "tock"]).cycle(2).to_a puts "cycled 2 times: #{cycled}" with_idx = Iterator.of(["alpha", "beta", "gamma"]).with_index(1).to_a puts "with_index(1): #{with_idx}" # 6. Terminals: fold, count, search nums = Iterator.of([10, 20, 30, 40]) sum = nums.reduce(0) { |acc, x| acc + x } puts "reduce sum: #{sum}" items = Iterator.of([1, 5, 12, 8, 3, 19]) greater_than_ten = items.find { |x| x > 10 } puts "first > 10: #{greater_than_ten}"
files.samples/iyi/std_text.iyi: # Standard text processing library demonstration. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/std_text.iyi import std/text # 1. Whitespace stripping and line cleaning raw_line = " \tGET /api/v1/users HTTP/1.1\r\n" cleaned = raw_line.strip.chomp puts "cleaned line: '#{cleaned}'" # 2. Splitting and partitioning parts = cleaned.split method = parts[0] path = parts[1] version = parts[2] puts "HTTP method: #{method}, path: #{path}, version: #{version}" key_val = "Authorization: Bearer token123".partition(": ") header_name = key_val[0] header_val = key_val[2] puts "Header '#{header_name}' = '#{header_val}'" # 3. Substitutions and transformations slug = "Hello World! This is iyi std/text.".downcase.tr(" /.", "---").delete("!") puts "slug: #{slug}" # 4. UTF-8 multi-byte handling greeting = "héllo world" puts "greeting size: #{greeting.size} characters, #{greeting.bytesize} bytes" puts "reversed greeting: #{greeting.reverse}" # 5. Base conversion hex_color = "ff" puts "hex '#{hex_color}' to decimal: #{hex_color.to_i(16)}"
files.samples/iyi/std_time.iyi: # Demonstrates `std/time`: wall clock, monotonic stopwatch, civil calendar, and RFC 3339. # # Run via: # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/std_time.iyi module samples/std_time import std/time using std/time::{Time, Span} # 1. Fixed reference date demonstration ref_time = Time.utc(2024, 2, 29, 12, 30, 45, 123) puts "Reference time (UTC): #{ref_time.to_s}" puts "RFC 3339: #{ref_time.to_rfc3339(3)}" puts "Unix timestamp: #{ref_time.to_unix} s (#{ref_time.to_unix_ms} ms)" # 2. Civil calendar components puts "Year: #{ref_time.year}" puts "Month: #{ref_time.month}" puts "Day: #{ref_time.day}" puts "Day of week: #{ref_time.day_of_week.to_s}" puts "Day of year: #{ref_time.day_of_year}" # 3. Time arithmetic with Span one_day = Span.days(1_i64) tomorrow = ref_time + one_day yesterday = ref_time - one_day puts "Tomorrow: #{tomorrow.to_rfc3339}" puts "Yesterday: #{yesterday.to_rfc3339}" # 4. Live clock queries (wall clock and monotonic stopwatch) now = Time.utc puts "Live wall clock valid: #{now.year >= 2024}" start = Time.monotonic # Burn a few cycles to measure elapsed duration acc = 0_i64 i = 0 while i < 100000 acc = acc + i.to_i64 i = i + 1 end elapsed = Time.monotonic - start puts "Monotonic duration >= 0: #{elapsed.total_seconds >= 0.0}" # 5. Parsing RFC 3339 strings event = Time.parse_rfc3339("2024-02-29T12:00:00Z") puts "Leap day event: #{event.to_s}" puts "Is leap year: #{Time.leap_year?(event.year)}"
files.samples/iyi/visited.iyi: # The first program that remembers what it has seen - a walk over a graph # with cycles in it, which ends only because it keeps a set of where it # has been. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/visited.iyi # # A `Hash` answers "what is this key's value"; a walk asks a smaller # question, "have I been here", and asks it of every neighbour of every # node. `Set` is that question with nothing attached to the answer: `add` # says whether the element was new, which is the one bit a walk needs, # and the set prints in the order things went in, so the path reads back # as a path. Like the six programs before it, this documents no rule: it # is here because the prelude grows only when a program asks (SPEC.md # 0.1.0 item 3), and the seventh program asks for a set. module samples/visited # Who links to whom. `docs` links back to `home`, which is the cycle a # walk without memory would never leave. links = { "home" => ["docs", "blog"], "docs" => ["install", "home"], "blog" => ["docs", "about"], "install" => [] of String, "about" => ["home"], "orphan" => ["home"], } of String => Array(String) # Everything reachable from `start`, breadth first, each page once. def reachable(links : Hash(String, Array(String)), start : String) : Set(String) seen = Set(String).new seen.add(start) queue = [start] while page = queue.shift? (links[page]? || [] of String).each do |next_page| queue << next_page if seen.add(next_page) end end seen end from_home = reachable(links, "home") puts from_home # => Set{"home", "docs", "blog", "install", "about"} puts from_home.size # => 5 puts from_home.includes?("orphan") # => false puts reachable(links, "install") # => Set{"install"} # The pages nobody reaches from home, which is the set difference. everything = Set(String).new links.each { |page, _| everything.add(page) } puts everything - from_home # => Set{"orphan"} # `add` answers whether the element was new: the second time is false. tags = Set(String).new puts tags.add("iyi") # => true puts tags.add("iyi") # => false puts tags.delete("iyi") # => true puts tags.empty? # => true # And the everyday shape of the same question: a list with repeats, # read into a set and back out, first occurrence wins. words = "the cat and the dog and the bird".split(' ') puts words.to_set.to_a # => ["the", "cat", "and", "dog", "bird"]
files.samples/iyi/webapp.iyi: # The Sinatra feel, kept — but written by the consumer rather than injected by # the library. This is the whole argument of SPEC.md II.3 in one file. module samples/webapp import kemal/dsl import kemal/router using kemal/dsl using kemal/router::{Router, Context} before_all do |env| nil end get "/" do |env| "home" end get "/users" do |env| "all users" end post "/users" do |env| "created" end # A route may return anything implementing `IntoBody`, which is strictly more # than Kemal allows: Kemal coerces non-String results to "" at runtime. get "/count" do |env| 42 end # A route returning a type with no impl is refused where it is written: # # get "/bad" do |env| # [1, 2, 3] # end # # => Array(Int32) does not implement Kemal::Router::IntoBody, # # required by `B` in `get` # # Kemal cannot say this. `HTTP::Server::Context -> _` accepts the block and # silently returns an empty body on every request. users = Router.new users.get "/" do |env| "users index" end # The sub-router is a block parameter rather than the block's `self`: R-2 asks # an exported `def` to describe its block, and a block whose `self` changes is # the one shape no annotation can describe yet. See `kemal/router.iyi`. users.namespace "/admin" do |admin| admin.get "/dashboard" do |env| "dashboard" end end mount "/v1", users app.routes.each { |route| puts "#{route[0]} #{route[1]}" } puts app.dispatch(Context.new("GET", "/count"))
files.samples/iyi/workers.iyi: # The first program with tasks in it - SPEC.md III.4, as a person writes it. # # ./bin/iyi run samples/iyi/workers.iyi # # Two shapes cover most of what a program wants from concurrency. A pool: # jobs go down one channel, workers answer up another, and the group's end # is the join. A pair: two things fetched at once, the group typed by what # they answer, so an error from either leaves as an ordinary member of the # union (III.4.3, III.4.9). Nothing here is a rule the other samples do not # state; it is the two programs a person writes first. module samples/workers # 1. A pool of three workers over six jobs. jobs = Channel(Int32).new(8) results = Channel(Int32).new(8) group do |g| 3.times do g.spawn do loop do case jobs.receive in Int32 then results.send(it * it) in ChannelClosed then break # no more jobs: this worker is done in Cancelled then break end end 0 end end g.spawn do (1..6).each { |n| jobs.send(n) } jobs.close 0 end total = 0 6.times do case results.receive in Int32 then total += it in ChannelClosed then break in Cancelled then break end end puts total # => 91, the squares of one to six end # The group's `end` waited for every worker: none outlives the scope that # started it (III.4.1). # 2. Two fetches at once, and the pair or the first error. struct Timeout def initialize(@what : String) end end impl Error for Timeout def message : String "#{@what} timed out" end end def read(name : String) : String | Timeout return Timeout.new(name) if name == "slow" "<#{name}>" end # `end!` makes the group a value: the tuple of what the two tasks answered, # or the first error member. `Panicked` is there because a task that panics # answers it (III.1.4), and the signature says so. def both(a : String, b : String) : Tuple(String, String) | Timeout | Panicked group do |g| x = g.spawn { read(a) } y = g.spawn { read(b) } end! end case both("one", "two") in Tuple(String, String) then puts it # => {"<one>", "<two>"} in Timeout then puts it.message in Panicked then puts "panicked" end case both("one", "slow") in Tuple(String, String) then puts it in Timeout then puts it.message # => slow timed out in Panicked then puts "panicked" end
files.samples/tour/arrays.iyi: # Arrays: ordered, growable, one element type. numbers = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] puts numbers.size puts numbers[0] puts numbers.first puts numbers.last numbers << 9 # append puts numbers # The common questions. puts numbers.includes?(4) puts numbers.sum puts numbers.sorted puts numbers.select { |n| n > 2 } puts numbers.map { |n| n * 10 } puts numbers.reduce(0) { |acc, n| acc + n } # An empty array needs its element type written down. names = [] of String names << "Ayşe" names << "Mehmet" puts names.join(", ") # Walk with an index. names.each_with_index { |name, i| puts "#{i + 1}. #{name}" }
files.samples/tour/blocks.iyi: # Blocks and closures: code you hand to a function. # `yield` runs the block the caller passed. def repeat(times : Int32) times.times { |i| yield i } end repeat(3) { |i| puts "step #{i}" } # A block sees the variables around it. total = 0 [1, 2, 3].each { |n| total += n } puts total # `->` makes a function value you can store and call later. square = ->(x : Int32) { x * x } puts square.call(7) # It captures its surroundings too: this one counts every call. count = 0 tick = ->() { count += 1 } tick.call tick.call puts count # A block parameter with a type, handed on as a value. def apply(x : Int32, &f : Int32 -> Int32) : Int32 f.call(x) end puts apply(5) { |v| v + 100 }
files.samples/tour/bounds.iyi: # Bounds: a generic that asks its type parameter for a trait. trait Priced abstract def price : Int32 end struct Book def initialize(@price : Int32) end end struct Coffee def initialize(@price : Int32) end end impl Priced for Book def price : Int32 @price end end impl Priced for Coffee def price : Int32 @price end end # `T : Priced` says: any T, as long as it implements Priced. The bound is # checked where the call is made, so `total([1, 2])` would not compile. def total(items : Array(T)) : Int32 forall T : Priced items.sum { |item| item.price } end puts total([Book.new(120), Book.new(80)]) puts total([Coffee.new(45)]) def cheapest(items : Array(T)) : T forall T : Priced items.min_by { |item| item.price } end puts cheapest([Coffee.new(45), Coffee.new(30)]).price
files.samples/tour/case.iyi: # `case`: one value, many branches. def day_kind(day : String) : String case day when "Saturday", "Sunday" then "weekend" when "Friday" then "almost" else "weekday" end end puts day_kind("Sunday") puts day_kind("Friday") puts day_kind("Tuesday") # A `case` with no value tests each condition in turn. score = 87 case when score >= 90 then puts "A" when score >= 80 then puts "B" else puts "C" end # `case ... in` matches on type, and it must cover every possibility. # `it` is the value, already narrowed to the branch's type. value = score > 50 ? 1 : "one" case value in Int32 then puts "a number: #{it + 1}" in String then puts "a word: #{it.upcase}" end
files.samples/tour/channels.iyi: # Channels: tasks talk by sending values, not by sharing them. jobs = Channel(Int32).new(8) results = Channel(Int32).new(8) group do |g| # Two workers. Each takes jobs until the channel closes. 2.times do g.spawn do loop do case jobs.receive in Int32 then results.send(it * 10) in ChannelClosed then break in Cancelled then break end end 0 end end # One producer. Closing says there will be no more. g.spawn do (1..5).each { |n| jobs.send(n) } jobs.close 0 end # Collect five answers. total = 0 5.times do case results.receive in Int32 then total += it in ChannelClosed then break in Cancelled then break end end puts total end
files.samples/tour/classes.iyi: # A class is a reference: two names can point at one object. class Counter # `property` makes a field readable and writable from outside. property count : Int32 def initialize(@count : Int32) end def bump : Nil @count += 1 end end a = Counter.new(0) b = a # b is the same counter, not a copy b.bump b.bump puts a.count # 2: the change is visible through a # A struct behaves differently: `b = a` would copy, and `a` stays at 0. # Use a struct for small values, a class for things that have identity. struct Cell property value : Int32 def initialize(@value : Int32) end end x = Cell.new(0) y = x y.value = 5 puts x.value # 0
files.samples/tour/conditions.iyi: # Conditions: `if`, `elsif`, `else`, `unless`, and `if` as a value. temperature = 23 if temperature > 30 puts "hot" elsif temperature > 20 puts "warm" else puts "cold" end # `unless` is `if not`. unless temperature < 0 puts "above freezing" end # A one-line form goes after the statement. puts "nice day" if temperature == 23 # `if` is an expression, so it can be assigned. label = if temperature > 20 "warm" else "cool" end puts label # The short form: condition ? when true : when false. puts temperature.even? ? "even" : "odd" # `&&`, `||`, `!` combine conditions. puts temperature > 20 && temperature < 30 puts !(temperature > 20)
files.samples/tour/constants.iyi: # Constants: a capitalised name, assigned once. PI = 3.14159 GREETING = "Merhaba" LIMIT = 100 def circle_area(r : Float64) : Float64 PI * r * r end puts circle_area(2.0).round(2) puts "#{GREETING}, dünya" puts LIMIT > 99
files.samples/tour/conversions.iyi: # Conversions are explicit: nothing changes type on its own. n = 42 puts n.to_f puts n.to_s + "!" f = 9.99 puts f.to_i puts f.round(1) # From text. `to_i` expects a number; `to_i?` answers nil when there is none. puts "17".to_i + 1 puts "17".to_i? puts "seventeen".to_i? # A Char is a byte, and its code is a number. puts 'A'.ord puts 66.chr
files.samples/tour/defaults.iyi: # Default methods: a trait can carry bodies of its own. trait Greet abstract def name : String # Not abstract: every implementer gets this one for free, written in # terms of the requirement. def greeting : String "Merhaba, #{name}!" end def shout : String greeting.upcase end end struct Person def initialize(@name : String) end end impl Greet for Person def name : String @name end end struct Robot def initialize(@id : Int32) end end impl Greet for Robot def name : String "unit #{@id}" end # An implementer may replace a default. def greeting : String "BEEP #{name}" end end puts Person.new("Ada").greeting puts Person.new("Ada").shout puts Robot.new(7).greeting puts Robot.new(7).shout
files.samples/tour/defer.iyi: # `defer`: name the cleanup where you acquire, run it when the scope ends. def work : Int32 puts "open" defer puts "close" puts "working" 42 end puts work # Deferred lines run last-in, first-out. def nested : Nil defer puts "third" defer puts "second" puts "first" end nested # The scope is the block, so in a loop the cleanup runs every turn. 2.times do |i| defer puts "done with #{i}" puts "turn #{i}" end
files.samples/tour/dispatch.iyi: # A trait is a type: one list, many kinds, one question. trait Speak abstract def sound : String end struct Dog def initialize(@name : String) end def name : String @name end end struct Cat def initialize(@name : String) end def name : String @name end end impl Speak for Dog def sound : String "hav" end end impl Speak for Cat def sound : String "miyav" end end # `of Speak` types the array by the trait, so both fit. animals = [Dog.new("Karabaş"), Cat.new("Pamuk")] of Speak animals.each { |animal| puts animal.sound } # A function can ask for the trait rather than a particular type. def chorus(voices : Array(Speak)) : String voices.map { |v| v.sound }.join(" ") end puts chorus(animals)
files.samples/tour/errors.iyi: # Errors are values. A function that can fail says so in its type. struct NotFound def initialize(@key : String) end def key : String @key end end # `Error` is a trait the compiler knows. Implementing it makes a type an # error member wherever it appears in a union. impl Error for NotFound def message : String "no such key: #{key}" end end STORE = {"name" => "iyi", "year" => "2026"} def fetch(key : String) : String | NotFound STORE[key]? || NotFound.new(key) end # `!` propagates: a good value continues, an error returns from here. def year_plus_one : Int32 | NotFound text = fetch("year")! text.to_i + 1 end puts year_plus_one # Handle with `case`, or fall back with `.or`, or insist with `.or_panic`. case fetch("missing") in String then puts it in NotFound then puts it.message end puts fetch("missing").or("default") puts fetch("name").or_panic
files.samples/tour/exports.iyi: # `using`: bring a module's exported names into this file unqualified. import geometry/point # The whole surface, or a chosen few in braces. Either way it is this file # that asks: a library cannot put names into a file that did not. using geometry/point::{Point, distance} home = Point.new(0, 0) work = Point.new(3, 4) puts distance(home, work) # `secret` was declared without `pub`, so it is not there to be found. # Uncomment the next line to see the compiler say so: # puts Geometry::Point.secret
files.samples/tour/functions.iyi: # Functions: `def`, typed parameters, a typed result. def add(a : Int32, b : Int32) : Int32 a + b end # The last expression is the result. There is no `return` needed. def describe(n : Int32) : String if n < 0 "negative" elsif n == 0 "zero" else "positive" end end # Parameters can have defaults, and callers can name them. def greet(name : String, greeting = "Hello") : String "#{greeting}, #{name}!" end puts add(2, 3) puts describe(-5) puts greet("Ayşe") puts greet("Ayşe", greeting: "Selam")
files.samples/tour/generic-functions.iyi: # Generic functions: `forall T` makes a function work for any type. def first(items : Array(T)) : T forall T items[0] end puts first([10, 20, 30]) puts first(["a", "b"]) def swap(pair : Tuple(A, B)) : Tuple(B, A) forall A, B {pair[1], pair[0]} end puts swap({1, "one"}) # The type is fixed per call: `first` of an Int32 array is an Int32, so # arithmetic on the result compiles. puts first([1, 2]) + 100
files.samples/tour/generic-types.iyi: # Generic types: a struct with a type parameter. struct Stack(T) def initialize @items = [] of T end def push(item : T) : Nil @items << item end def pop : T? @items.empty? ? nil : @items.pop end def size : Int32 @items.size end end numbers = Stack(Int32).new numbers.push(1) numbers.push(2) puts numbers.size puts numbers.pop puts numbers.pop puts numbers.pop words = Stack(String).new words.push("iyi") puts words.pop # A trait can be implemented for the generic type once, for every T. trait Describe abstract def describe : String end impl Describe for Stack(T) forall T def describe : String "a stack of #{size}" end end numbers.push(5) puts numbers.describe puts words.describe
files.samples/tour/geometry/point.iyi: # A module other files can import. Its path is its name. module geometry/point # `pub` makes a declaration part of the module's surface. An exported # declaration writes its types down, so a file that imports this one # never has to read the body. pub struct Point getter x : Int32 getter y : Int32 def initialize(@x : Int32, @y : Int32) end end pub def distance(a : Point, b : Point) : Int32 (a.x - b.x).abs + (a.y - b.y).abs end # No `pub`: this name is the module's own and cannot be reached from outside. def secret : String "only here" end
files.samples/tour/hashes.iyi: # Hashes: keys to values, in insertion order. ages = {"Ayşe" => 31, "Mehmet" => 27} puts ages["Ayşe"] puts ages.size ages["Zeynep"] = 40 puts ages.keys # `[]?` answers nil for a missing key instead of failing. puts ages["Ali"]? puts ages.has_key?("Ali") ages.each do |name, age| puts "#{name} is #{age}" end # An empty hash needs both types written down. counts = {} of String => Int32 ["a", "b", "a"].each do |letter| counts[letter] = (counts[letter]? || 0) + 1 end puts counts
files.samples/tour/hello.iyi: # Your first iyi program. puts "Hello Türkiye!"
files.samples/tour/loops.iyi: # Loops: `each` over a collection, `times`, `while`, and `loop`. [1, 2, 3].each do |n| puts n end 3.times { |i| puts "round #{i}" } n = 1 while n < 50 n = n * 2 end puts n # `loop` runs until `break`. `next` skips to the next turn. count = 0 loop do count += 1 next if count == 2 puts "count #{count}" break if count == 4 end
files.samples/tour/methods.iyi: # Methods: functions that belong to a type. struct Rectangle getter width : Float64 getter height : Float64 def initialize(@width : Float64, @height : Float64) end def area : Float64 width * height end def square? : Bool width == height end # A method can take arguments like any function. def scale(factor : Float64) : Rectangle Rectangle.new(width * factor, height * factor) end end r = Rectangle.new(3.0, 4.0) puts r.area puts r.square? puts r.scale(2.0).area # Methods on the built-in types work the same way. puts "iyi".upcase puts 3.7.round puts [1, 2, 3].sum
files.samples/tour/modules.iyi: # Modules: every file is one, and `import` brings another in. # `geometry/point` is the file geometry/point.iyi. The path is the name. import geometry/point # After `import`, the module's exports are reachable under its qualified # name: the path with each segment capitalised, joined by `::`. a = Geometry::Point::Point.new(1, 2) b = Geometry::Point::Point.new(4, 6) puts Geometry::Point.distance(a, b)
files.samples/tour/nil.iyi: # nil is a value, and the type says whether it can appear. # `String?` is `String | Nil`: it may hold a string, or nothing. def lookup(id : Int32) : String? id == 1 ? "Ada" : nil end found = lookup(1) missing = lookup(2) puts found puts missing # Before you use a maybe-nil value, check it. Inside the `if`, the # compiler knows it is a String. if found puts found.upcase end # Or give a default with `||`. puts missing || "nobody" # Calling a String method on a `String?` without checking does not # compile. That is the whole point: a nil can never surprise you at run time.
files.samples/tour/ranges.iyi: # Ranges: `..` includes the end, `...` stops before it. (1..5).each { |i| puts i } (1...5).each { |i| puts i } # A range is a collection: map, sum, select, to_a all work. puts (1..5).map { |i| i * i } puts (1..100).sum puts (1..10).select { |i| i % 3 == 0 } # Ranges also work in a `case`. age = 42 case age when 0..12 then puts "child" when 13..19 then puts "teen" else puts "adult" end
files.samples/tour/returns.iyi: # More than one result: a tuple, unpacked at the call. def divide(a : Int32, b : Int32) : Tuple(Int32, Int32) {a // b, a % b} end quotient, remainder = divide(17, 5) puts quotient puts remainder # A tuple is a value like any other. pair = divide(9, 4) puts pair[0] puts pair[1] # `return` leaves early, and can carry a value. def first_even(numbers : Array(Int32)) : Int32? numbers.each do |n| return n if n % 2 == 0 end nil end puts first_even([1, 3, 6, 7]) puts first_even([1, 3])
files.samples/tour/strings.iyi: # Strings, and `to_s`: how a type says what it looks like. s = "Hello, iyi" puts s.size puts s.upcase puts s.downcase puts s.includes?("iyi") puts s + "!" puts s.split(' ') # Interpolation calls `to_s` on whatever is inside `#{}`. puts "#{1 + 1} and #{true} and #{[1, 2]}" # Give your own type a `to_s`, and it prints the way you say. struct Money def initialize(@lira : Int32, @kurus : Int32) end def to_s : String "#{@lira},#{@kurus.to_s.rjust(2, '0')} TL" end end price = Money.new(12, 5) puts price.to_s puts "total: #{price}" # Padding lines up columns. puts "item".ljust(8) + "12" puts "total".ljust(8) + "99"
files.samples/tour/structs.iyi: # A struct: named fields, a constructor, methods. struct Point getter x : Int32 getter y : Int32 # `@x` is the field. Writing it in the parameter list assigns it. def initialize(@x : Int32, @y : Int32) end def +(other : Point) : Point Point.new(x + other.x, y + other.y) end def to_s : String "(#{x}, #{y})" end end a = Point.new(1, 2) b = Point.new(3, 4) puts a.x puts (a + b).to_s # A struct is a value: assigning it copies it. c = a puts c.to_s
files.samples/tour/tasks.iyi: # Tasks: run work at the same time, inside a group that waits for it all. def slow_square(n : Int32) : Int32 sleep 10 # milliseconds n * n end # `group` opens a scope. Every `spawn` inside it is a task, and the # group's `end` waits for every one of them: no task outlives its group. results = [] of Int32 group do |g| (1..4).each do |n| g.spawn do results << slow_square(n) 0 end end end puts results.sorted # `end!` turns the group into a value: the tuple of what its tasks answered. def both : Tuple(String, String) | Panicked group do |g| a = g.spawn { "first" } b = g.spawn { "second" } end! end case both in Tuple(String, String) then puts it in Panicked then puts "a task panicked" end
files.samples/tour/traits.iyi: # A trait: a set of methods a type promises to have. trait Shape # `abstract def` is a requirement. Every implementer must define it. abstract def area : Float64 end struct Circle def initialize(@radius : Float64) end end struct Square def initialize(@side : Float64) end end # `impl Trait for Type` is the one way to give a type a trait. The impl # lives next to the trait or next to the type, never anywhere else. impl Shape for Circle def area : Float64 3.14159 * @radius * @radius end end impl Shape for Square def area : Float64 @side * @side end end puts Circle.new(1.0).area.round(2) puts Square.new(2.0).area # Leave a requirement out and the compiler refuses the impl, naming the # missing method. Try removing `area` from one of the impls above.
files.samples/tour/tuples.iyi: # Tuples: a fixed group of values, each with its own type. pair = {1, "one"} puts pair[0] puts pair[1] # Unpack into variables. number, word = pair puts "#{number} is #{word}" # A named tuple gives each slot a name. person = {name: "Ayşe", age: 31} puts person[:name] puts person[:age] # A function that answers several things at once. def min_max(items : Array(Int32)) : Tuple(Int32, Int32) low = items.first high = items.first items.each do |n| low = n if n < low high = n if n > high end {low, high} end low, high = min_max([7, 2, 9, 4]) puts "#{low}..#{high}"
files.samples/tour/types.iyi: # The basic types, and what each literal is. i = 42 # Int32 big = 4_000_000_000_i64 # Int64, with a suffix f = 3.14 # Float64 b = true # Bool c = 'a' # Char s = "text" # String puts typeof(i) puts typeof(big) puts typeof(f) puts typeof(b) puts typeof(c) puts typeof(s) # Integer arithmetic stays integer with `//`; `/` gives a Float64. puts 7 // 2 puts 7 / 2 puts 7 % 2 puts 2 ** 10
files.samples/tour/unions.iyi: # Union types: a value that is one of several types. # `Int32 | String` holds either. Nothing is wrapped or boxed. def parse(text : String) : Int32 | String n = text.to_i? n ? n : "not a number: #{text}" end # `case ... in` must name every member, so a new member in the union # turns every incomplete `case` into a compile error. ["12", "x", "7"].each do |text| case parse(text) in Int32 then puts "number #{it * 2}" in String then puts "problem, #{it}" end end # `is_a?` asks, and narrows inside the `if`. value = parse("5") if value.is_a?(Int32) puts value + 1 end # `String?` from the nil lesson is the same idea: `String | Nil`.
files.samples/tour/variables.iyi: # Variables: assign a value and the type follows. name = "iyi" year = 2026 ratio = 0.75 ready = true puts name puts year puts ratio puts ready # A variable keeps its type. You can reassign, but not to a different kind. year = year + 1 puts year # Write the type when you want to be explicit. count : Int32 = 10 puts count
files.records/break/dep/global_derive.iyi: # A module the break program imports, exporting one derive macro. It compiles: # a macro body is expanded where the `derive` is written, not where the macro # is defined, so the refusal this module earns lands in its consumer's build. # # `counted` asks a question about the whole program. `all_subclasses` answers # with every type compiled beside it, which is exactly what R-5 keeps a macro # away from: a derive that read it would generate different code depending on # what else happened to be in the build, and then a `.iyimod` could not carry # what it generated (SPEC.md R-5, II.4). module dep/global_derive pub macro counted(declaration) def counted : Int32 {% count = 0 %} {% for field in declaration[:fields] %} {% count = field[:type].all_subclasses.size %} {% end %} {{ count }} end end
files.records/break/dep/greeter.iyi: # A module the break programs import. Its surface is deliberately narrow: one # exported function, one exported trait, and one function left unexported so a # consumer has something it is not allowed to reach. module dep/greeter pub trait Greet abstract def greet : String end pub def polite(name : String) : String "#{greeting}, #{name}." end # No `pub`, so this is the module's own business. It is not in the module's # declarations, which is what makes reaching for it from another module an # error rather than a style question (SPEC.md R-1, IV.2). def greeting : String "Hello" end
files.records/break/dep/loop_a.iyi: # Half of a deliberate import cycle. See `../r1_import_cycle.iyi`. module dep/loop_a import dep/loop_b pub def a : String "a" end
files.records/break/dep/loop_b.iyi: # The other half of the cycle. `dep/loop_a` imports this module and this # module imports `dep/loop_a`, which is the edge that closes it. module dep/loop_b import dep/loop_a pub def b : String "b" end
files.records/break/dep/user.iyi: # A second module the break programs import, so that a trait and a type can # live in two different places and an impl can be written in a third. module dep/user pub struct User getter name : String def initialize(@name : String) end end
files.records/break/errors_non_exhaustive.iyi: # Breaks the error rule in SPEC.md III.1: an error is an ordinary member of a # union, so handling one needs no new machinery, only the totality check a # `case` already performs. `read` can return an `IOError` and this `case` has # no branch for it, which is the same mistake as ignoring a returned error and # is caught by the same check. module diagnostics/errors_non_exhaustive pub struct IOError getter path : String def initialize(@path : String) end end # `Error` is the compiler's trait, which is what lets a union member be an # error member without any name in scope deciding it. impl Error for IOError def message : String "no such file: #{path}" end end pub def read(path : String) : String | IOError return IOError.new(path) if path == "missing" "12" end case read("missing") in String then puts it end
files.records/break/r1_import_cycle.iyi: # Breaks R-1: a module is the unit of compilation and `import` forms a DAG, so # the graph has to be acyclic for anything else to hold. A cycle has no # initialisation order, since a module initialises after every module it # imports and here each would have to follow the other, and the acyclicity is # also what makes at most one module able to define any given impl. `dep/loop_a` # and `dep/loop_b` import each other. module diagnostics/r1_import_cycle import dep/loop_a using dep/loop_a puts a
files.records/break/r2_missing_return_type.iyi: # Breaks R-2: everything a module exports carries full parameter and return # types, because the signature is the whole of what a consumer reads. Drop the # return type and there is nothing to write into the artifact, so the omission # is refused where it is written rather than inferred from the body. module diagnostics/r2_missing_return_type pub def total(numbers : Array(Int32)) numbers.sum end puts total([1, 2, 3])
files.records/break/r2_not_exported.iyi: # Breaks R-2: only what a module marks `pub` is reachable from outside it, and # `greeting` in `dep/greeter` carries no `pub`. Qualifying the call does not get # around that. It has to be genuinely unreachable rather than merely absent # from a `using`, because a `.iyimod` carries a module's exports and nothing # else, so if another module could call an unmarked name that artifact would # not be enough to compile against. module diagnostics/r2_not_exported import dep/greeter puts Dep::Greeter.greeting
files.records/break/r2_wrong_return_type.iyi: # Breaks R-2 the other way: the type is written, and the body does not honour # it. An exported signature is a promise to every consumer that reads the # artifact instead of the body, so the body is the thing that has to give. module diagnostics/r2_wrong_return_type pub def total(numbers : Array(Int32)) : Int32 numbers.join(",") end puts total([1, 2, 3])
files.records/break/r2b_using_missing.iyi: # Breaks R-2b: `import` brings a module into scope under its qualified name and # nothing more. Unqualified names arrive only through a `using`, which the # consumer writes, so importing a module never quietly changes what a name in # this file means. `polite` is exported and still not in scope here. module diagnostics/r2b_using_missing import dep/greeter puts polite("iyi")
files.records/break/r2c_outside_bound.iyi: # Breaks R-2c: a def whose parameters and return are all written is typed at # its definition, caller or no caller, and a trait-restricted parameter is # typed against exactly its bound. Two halves of the rule fail here at once. # # Nothing in this file calls `loudest`, so under the lazy typing iyi inherited # from Crystal its body would never be visited and the build would report # itself clean. And `User`, the only implementer of `Greet` in the program, has # a `shout` of its own: duck-typed generics would have found it and compiled. # `Greet` declares `greet` and nothing else, so the body reaches outside the # bound it wrote down, and the message names the witness type the compiler # synthesized to type it (SPEC.md R-2c; # src/compiler/iyi/semantic/definition_typing.cr). module diagnostics/r2c_outside_bound pub trait Greet abstract def greet : String end pub struct User getter name : String def initialize(@name : String) end # Present on the concrete type, and irrelevant to the def below: the bound is # what that body is typed against, not whatever happens to implement it. def shout : String "HELLO" end end impl Greet for User def greet : String "Hello, #{name}." end end pub def loudest(g : Greet) : String g.shout end
files.records/break/r3_orphan_impl.iyi: # Breaks R-3: `impl Trait for Type` may live in the module that defines the # trait or the module that defines the type, and nowhere else. `Greet` belongs # to `dep/greeter` and `User` belongs to `dep/user`, so this module owns # neither and is the one place the impl cannot be written. That restriction is # what makes a type's method set knowable from its declarations alone. module diagnostics/r3_orphan_impl import dep/greeter import dep/user using dep/greeter using dep/user impl Greet for User def greet : String "Hello, #{name}." end end puts User.new("iyi").greet
files.records/break/r3_unmet_trait_bound.iyi: # Breaks R-3 from the calling side: a type's method set is closed, so a bound # on a type parameter is a question with a definite answer at the call. `Int32` # has no `impl Greet` and cannot acquire one later, so the call is refused as a # missing trait rather than as a failed overload match. module diagnostics/r3_unmet_trait_bound pub trait Greet abstract def greet : String end pub struct User getter name : String def initialize(@name : String) end end impl Greet for User def greet : String "Hello, #{name}." end end pub def announce(item : T) : String forall T : Greet "-> #{item.greet}" end puts announce(User.new("iyi")) puts announce(42)
files.records/break/r4_dictionary.iyi: # Breaks R-4 by asking for the one clause of it that has nothing behind it. # # R-4's third sentence says `@[Monomorphize]` forces specialisation across a # module boundary. SPEC.md III.9 records what that is worth today: nothing in # the compiler mentions the annotation, a dictionary or a GC shape. So this is # not a feature that misbehaves, it is a name the compiler has never heard, # and the rejection below is a compiler declining to accept a promise it # cannot keep rather than compiling the program as though the rule were built. # # What runs instead of the dictionary is the rule's second sentence applied # everywhere: a generic's body travels in the artifact and every consumer # compiles it again for the types it uses. `bench/generic_boundary.py` is the # measurement of what that costs a consumer's front end. module diagnostics/r4_dictionary @[Monomorphize] pub def twice(x : T) : Array(T) forall T [x, x] end puts twice(1).size
files.records/break/r5_global_question.iyi: # Breaks R-5: a macro sees the declaration it is attached to, and nothing # global. Everything here is legal. `Point` is this module's own type, the # derive is written inside its body where a derive belongs, and `counted` # comes from a module this file imports and `using`s, which is the only way a # derive macro can arrive. What is refused is the one question the macro asks: # `all_subclasses` answers with the whole program rather than with this # declaration, so the answer would depend on what else was compiled and the # methods it generated could not travel in this module's artifact. # # The refusal lands at expansion, in the consumer's build, which is where the # macro runs. `dep/global_derive.iyi` is the macro (SPEC.md R-5, II.4). module diagnostics/r5_global_question import dep/global_derive using dep/global_derive pub struct Point @x : Int32 def initialize(@x : Int32) end derive counted end puts Point.new(1).counted
files.records/agent/app/greeter.iyi: # The dependency. Its exported surface is the whole of what a consumer, or an # agent editing one, is allowed to know: two functions with their types # written down, and a trait. `greeting` has no `pub`, so it is this module's # own business and appears in no consumer's grounding (SPEC.md R-1, IV.2). module app/greeter pub trait Greet abstract def greet : String end # The exported surface carries its doc comment, so the grounding pack an agent # reads says what the function is for and not only what it takes. pub def polite(name : String) : String "#{greeting}, #{name}." end pub def shout(name : String) : String "#{greeting.upcase}, #{name.upcase}!" end def greeting : String "Hello" end
files.records/agent/app.iyi: # The file being edited, in the state an agent meets it: one call misspelled. # The compiler knows the name it meant, so `iyi check -f json` carries a # `suggested_edit` with the exact replacement span and `iyi fix` applies it. module app import app/greeter using app/greeter pub def main : Int32 puts polit("Türkiye") 0 end
files.records/agent/app_test.iyi: # A test is a plain program that exits non-zero when it fails; the prelude's # `assert` is that in one word. No framework, so nothing here has to be # learned before it can be read. module app/app_test import app/greeter using app/greeter assert polite("iyi") == "Hello, iyi.", "polite greets" assert shout("iyi") == "HELLO, IYI!", "shout shouts"
